title: Photosynthesis: A Complete Section-Type Reference
overview: A reference lesson that exercises every section type in the Lesson contract, including timeline, diagram and chart, which the hand-written photosynthesis.lesson.json example does not cover. Built for backend/frontend integration work, not for display to students.
subject: biology

source_references.excerpt: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.

content.definition: The process in which plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen is released.
key_points: Inputs: carbon dioxide, water and light energy.

content.body: Photosynthesis happens inside chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll, a green pigment that absorbs red and blue light and reflects green light.
key_points: Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects green light.

source_references.excerpt: The Calvin cycle turns carbon dioxide into glucose in a series of steps.

steps.title: Fix carbon
steps.description: Carbon dioxide from the air is attached to an existing 5-carbon molecule.

steps.title: Reduce
steps.description: ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent reactions convert the fixed carbon into sugar precursors.

sections.title: Light-dependent reactions and the Calvin cycle

source_references.excerpt: confirmed the light and dark reactions
In 1930 Cornelis van Niel proposed the modern equation for photosynthesis.

events.title: Modern equation proposed
events.description: Cornelis van Niel proposed the modern equation for photosynthesis, based on studies of bacteria.

events.title: Two-stage process confirmed
events.description: Researchers confirmed the separate light-dependent and light-independent (Calvin cycle) stages.

content.scenario: A piece of pondweed is placed in water under a lamp. Small bubbles form on its leaves; moving the lamp closer produces more bubbles per minute.
content.explanation: The bubbles are mostly oxygen released by photosynthesis. Moving the lamp closer increases light intensity, so photosynthesis happens faster, until another factor becomes the limit.

content.summary: Light powers the light-dependent reactions, which produce ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle uses them, plus carbon dioxide, to produce glucose.

sections.title: The Calvin cycle as a loop

source_references.excerpt: The Calvin cycle turns carbon dioxide into glucose in a series of steps.

content.summary: Carbon dioxide enters the cycle, is fixed and reduced using ATP and NADPH, and glucose precursors leave the cycle while the original 5-carbon molecule is regenerated.

nodes.label: Reduction
nodes.description: ATP and NADPH convert it to sugar precursors

sections.title: Bubbles per minute vs. distance from the lamp

source_references.excerpt: 12 bubbles formed per minute at 10 cm and 30 bubbles formed per minute at 5 cm from the lamp.

content.summary: Moving the lamp closer to the pondweed increased the rate of bubble formation, showing that light intensity was limiting the rate of photosynthesis at the greater distance.

quiz.prompt: Which gas do plants release during photosynthesis?
quiz.explanation: Water is split during the light-dependent reactions. Oxygen is released as a by-product.

quiz.prompt: Who proposed the modern equation for photosynthesis, and when?
quiz.explanation: Cornelis van Niel proposed the modern equation in 1930, based on studies of photosynthetic bacteria.

source_references.excerpt: In 1930 Cornelis van Niel proposed the modern equation

quiz.prompt: In the pondweed experiment, what happened to the bubble rate when the lamp moved from 10 cm to 5 cm?
quiz.explanation: The rate rose from 12 to 30 bubbles per minute as light intensity increased.
